explanations.explanation: Almost, friend, but the last three words matter. Paul, the writer of this letter, says Abraham would have something to boast about, “but not before God.” So the bragging might fly with other people, but it gets nowhere with God. I once tried boasting about my stamping to a cooling rack. It didn't clap.

You caught the key words, friend. Paul says that if Abraham was justified by works, he would have something to boast about, “but not before God.” So the boasting goes nowhere with God either way. A trophy that nobody in the room will look at is just a shiny paperweight.

That's it, friend. The Scripture Paul quotes says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.” Believing is what the verse names, and that's the whole thing. Paul doesn't even need a second sentence for it.

I get the thought, friend, because keeping the law sounds like what earns a gold star. But the Scripture Paul quotes doesn't say that. It says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.” The verse names believing, so that's where we stay.

Building an altar takes real effort, friend, and I respect a good building project. But that's not what the Scripture Paul quotes names. It says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.” The credit went to his believing.

Yes, friend. Paul says, “Now the wages of the worker are not credited as a gift, but as an obligation.” If you put in the hours, the pay is owed to you. Nobody has ever hugged their boss for it, and I'd pay to watch somebody try.

An honor sounds nice, friend, like a medal on your apron. But Paul's word here is “obligation.” When a worker earns wages, they're owed, so they aren't a gift and they aren't a special honor. They're just what's due.

An advance is pay handed over before the work, friend, and that would be a fun Friday. But Paul says wages are credited “not as a gift, but as an obligation.” He means what the worker is owed for work already done.

That's the one, friend. Paul says the one who does not work “believes in Him who justifies the ungodly.” Read that slowly, because it's a big deal. His faith is credited as righteousness, and it was never wages.
That's what you'd expect if this were a paycheck, friend. But Paul's picture is about God, “Him who justifies the ungodly.” Nobody has to be deserving first. That's exactly the flip Paul is making.

Hard work earns wages, friend, and Paul just covered that in verse 4. Here he's talking about someone who “does not work, but believes.” That person believes in Him “who justifies the ungodly.” So the answer isn't a worker.

That's right, friend. Paul quotes David, king of Israel, who says, “Blessed are they whose lawless acts are forgiven, whose sins are covered.” Forgiven and covered, in the same breath. I know a thing or two about being covered in dust, but this is much better.

Repaid sounds like a bill getting settled, friend. But David, king of Israel, says something else in the words Paul quotes: “Blessed are they whose lawless acts are forgiven, whose sins are covered.” Forgiven and covered, with no repaying mentioned.

Being written down sounds like a long list, friend. But David, king of Israel, says in Paul's quote, “Blessed are they whose lawless acts are forgiven, whose sins are covered.” Covered is the word. Nobody is keeping a ledger in that line.

Careful, friend, because this one is flipped. David says, “Blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will never count against him.” Never. So the blessed man's sin isn't held up against him later. It's close to the opposite of what the statement says.

You've got it, friend. David says, “Blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will never count against him.” Never counted against him, not now and not later. That's about as far from a grudge as you can get.

That's right, friend. Paul says it plainly: “It was not after, but before.” Abraham's faith was credited while he was still uncircumcised. The order matters, because it shows the credit didn't come from the circumcision.

That's the order you'd guess if circumcision was the thing doing the work, friend. But Paul answers his own question: “It was not after, but before.” Abraham received circumcision as a sign later, “while he was still uncircumcised” when the righteousness was credited (Romans 4:11).

explanations.answer: On the day of his circumcision
explanations.explanation: A tidy answer, friend, with the credit and the circumcision landing together. But Paul says, “It was not after, but before.” He says Abraham had righteousness by faith “while he was still uncircumcised,” and the sign came as a seal of it.

That's right, friend. Abraham is “the father of all who believe but are not circumcised.” Since his faith came first, people who haven't been circumcised can still be counted as his children. That's a big family tree, and it grows on believing.

I see why work might jump out, friend, since we just had a whole paycheck talk. But Paul's word is “believe.” Abraham is “the father of all who believe but are not circumcised.” It's faith that makes the family, and there's no timecard.

Fasting isn't anywhere in this verse, friend. Paul says Abraham is “the father of all who believe but are not circumcised.” Believing is the word that fits the blank. I'll let my ovens do the fasting.

Exactly, friend. Paul says the circumcised are also Abraham's children when they “walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.” So being circumcised isn't the only thing. They walk in his faith's footsteps, and I love that picture.

Keeping the law might feel like the natural second marker, friend. But Paul doesn't say that here. He says they also “walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.” Faith is the footprint to follow.

explanations.answer: Living in the land of Canaan
explanations.explanation: Canaan is a good guess for a place tied to Abraham, friend, but Paul doesn't mention land in this verse. He says the circumcised are also his children when they “walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.” It's about his faith, not an address.

explanations.answer: The righteousness that comes by faith
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul says the promise “was not given through the law, but through the righteousness that comes by faith.” The promise was that Abraham and his offspring would be heir of the world. It came through faith, so there was no paperwork to fill out.

Years of service feels like it should earn something this big, friend. But Paul says the promise came “through the righteousness that comes by faith.” Service isn't named in that verse. The promise came the same way the credit did.

That's a thoughtful guess after all that circumcision talk, friend. But Paul says the promise came “through the righteousness that comes by faith.” Circumcision was a sign, “a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith” (Romans 4:11). The seal wasn't the source.

That's the word, friend. Paul says that if law-livers are the heirs, “faith is useless and the promise is worthless.” He plays out the other side to show it falls apart. If the promise depended on the law, faith would have nothing left to do.

Earned fits the way the law-livers might see it, friend. But the verse says, “faith is useless and the promise is worthless.” Paul uses “worthless” to show what happens if the heirs are those who live by the law. It breaks the promise instead of earning it.

Delayed would at least keep the promise alive, friend. But Paul goes further and says, “faith is useless and the promise is worthless.” He doesn't talk about timing here. He says the promise loses its value.
That's right, friend. Paul says, “the law brings wrath.” Then he adds, “And where there is no law, there is no transgression.” Those words are heavy, so I'll just leave them there.

That's what the verse says, friend, and Paul says it outright: “the law brings wrath.” He follows it with, “And where there is no law, there is no transgression.” So True is the answer here, and it's a heavy line to read.
Yes, friend. Paul says the promise comes by faith “so that it may rest on grace.” Grace is a gift, so nobody has to pay it back. I'll take a gift over a bill any day.

The law has been in this conversation all along, friend, so I get the pull. But Paul says the promise comes by faith “so that it may rest on grace.” In this verse the law isn't what the promise rests on. Grace is.
Works came up a lot earlier in the passage, friend, so it's a fair guess. But Paul says the promise comes by faith “so that it may rest on grace.” Works aren't the foundation here. Grace is.

That's right, friend. Paul says the promise is “guaranteed to all Abraham's offspring.” That includes “not only to those who are of the law, but also to those who are of the faith of Abraham.” Then he says, “He is the father of us all.”

explanations.answer: Only those who keep the law
explanations.explanation: That one leaves out half the family, friend. Paul says the promise is guaranteed to all Abraham's offspring, “not only to those who are of the law, but also to those who are of the faith of Abraham.” The word is not only. It goes wider than the law.

That makes the guest list very short, friend. Paul says the promise is guaranteed to “all Abraham's offspring,” which includes those “of the faith of Abraham.” He never mentions a firstborn son. The promise is for far more people than one.
Yes, friend. Paul calls Him “the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not yet exist.” Think about that for a second. Both of those are things only He does.

After the paycheck talk, I understand the guess, friend. But in this verse, Paul describes “the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not yet exist.” Rewarding the hardest workers isn't part of that line.

The wages picture was about a worker and his pay, friend, and that was back in verse 4. Here Paul describes the God Abraham believed as “the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not yet exist.” No wage book in sight.

It might sound like his faith worked by looking away, friend, but Paul says the opposite. He says Abraham “acknowledged the decrepitness of his body” since he was about a hundred years old, and he acknowledged “the lifelessness of Sarah's womb.” Sarah is Abraham's wife (Genesis 17:15). He looked right at it, and his faith did not weaken.

That's right, friend. Paul says Abraham “acknowledged the decrepitness of his body (since he was about a hundred years old) and the lifelessness of Sarah's womb.” Sarah is Abraham's wife (Genesis 17:15). He saw it clearly, and Paul says his faith did not weaken.

That's the word, friend. Paul says Abraham “did not waver through disbelief in the promise of God, but was strengthened in his faith and gave glory to God.” His faith got stronger, not smaller. And he gave God the glory, which is a good way to end a sentence.

Humbled is a believable word for a man at a hundred years old, friend, but it isn't Paul's. He says Abraham “did not waver through disbelief in the promise of God, but was strengthened in his faith and gave glory to God.” Strengthened is the word.

Tested sounds like it fits a hard situation, friend, but it's not the word here. Paul says Abraham “did not waver through disbelief in the promise of God, but was strengthened in his faith and gave glory to God.” His faith got stronger.

explanations.answer: God was able to do what He promised
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. Paul says Abraham was “fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised.” His confidence was in God's ability, not in his own. That's a very sturdy place to put it.

explanations.answer: God would reward him for his faithfulness
explanations.explanation: Rewards would be nice, friend, but Paul doesn't say that. He says Abraham was “fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised.” His persuasion was about what God was able to do.

explanations.answer: God would first explain how it would happen
explanations.explanation: I think I'd have asked for a diagram, friend. But Paul never says Abraham waited on an explanation. He says Abraham was “fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised.” He trusted that God could do it.

explanations.answer: Those who believe in Him who raised Jesus
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul says the words were written “for us, to whom righteousness will be credited—for us who believe in Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead.” That's how Abraham's story reaches us today. The same believing sits at the center.

explanations.answer: Those who keep every part of the law
explanations.explanation: Paul has just spent a lot of words saying the promise doesn't come that way, friend. He says righteousness will be credited to “us who believe in Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead.” It's believing again, not law-keeping.

explanations.answer: Those born into Abraham's family line
explanations.explanation: Family line is a natural thing to think of with Abraham, friend, but it isn't what Paul says here. He says righteousness will be credited to “us who believe in Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead.” Believing is what Paul points to.

That's the one, friend. Paul says Jesus “was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification.” He was delivered over for our trespasses, and He was raised for our justification. That's a good place to end the letter's big point.
I see why punishment might come up next to trespasses, friend. But Paul says Jesus “was raised to life for our justification.” Justification is the word for why He was raised.

Wages were all over this passage, friend, so I'm not surprised the word stuck. But Paul says Jesus “was raised to life for our justification.” Wages belong to the workers' side of the story, and this verse is about justification.
